items.title: The Silla Annals' Anachronistic Reference to Queen Himiko, the Wa Ruler of Yamatai
items.note: Examines the Samguk sagi's reference to a Himiko embassy dated to 173 CE and argues that the entry is anachronistic.

items.title: Kōkogaku kara mite Yamataikoku Yamato-setsu wa naritatsu ka? (Does the Yamato theory of Yamatai hold up archaeologically?)
items.note: A former Kashihara Institute archaeologist questions whether the archaeology of the Nara basin can support the Yamato theory.

items.title: Makimuku iseki shutsudo no momo no kaku no AMS 14C nendai sokutei (AMS radiocarbon dating of peach stones from the Makimuku site)
items.note: Dated twelve peach stones from a pit by the large Makimuku building complex to roughly 135–230 CE, presented as support for a Makimuku Yamatai.

items.title: Jiji koron 8: Makimuku iseki shutsudo no momo no kaku nendai sokutei (zenpen)
items.note: Detailed rebuttal of the peach-stone interpretation by a leading Kyushu-theory advocate, continued in 2019 and expanded into a book.

items.title: Namari dōitaihi ni yoru sankakuen shinjūkyō seisakuchi no kentō (The production place of triangular-rimmed mirrors examined through lead isotope ratios)
items.note: Uses lead isotope data to address whether the triangular-rimmed mirrors were made in Wei China or Japan, the crux of their value as evidence for Yamatai.

items.title: Kōkogaku kara mita Yamataikoku Yamato-setsu: Kinai de wa arienu Yamataikoku
items.note: Book-length archaeological case against a Kinai Yamatai, drawing on decades of excavation in Nara; widely discussed as an insider critique.

items.title: Sankakubuchi shinjūkyō seisakuchi dōtei e mukete (Toward identifying where the triangular-rimmed deity-and-beast mirrors were made), KAKEN JP20KK0010
items.note: JSPS grant (2020–2026, ¥18.59 million) surveying Han–Jin mirrors in Shandong with lead-isotope analysis to settle whether the mirrors linked to Himiko's Wei gift were made in China.

items.title: Makimuku iseki no shutsudozai nenrin nendai kettei ni mukete: sanso dōitaihi no nensōnai hendō kaiseki
items.note: Applies intra-ring oxygen isotope analysis to Makimuku timbers as a route to calendar dates independent of radiocarbon calibration.

items.title: Makimuku iseki shutsudo momo kaku no AMS 14C nendai no saishinban kōsei dēta IntCal20 ni yoru reki-nen kōsei
items.note: Recalibrated the Makimuku peach-stone dates with IntCal20, showing how the calendar range depends on the calibration curve used.

items.title: Himiko to Yamato ōken (Himiko and the Yamato kingship)
items.note: The director of the Makimuku research centre sets out the Kinai case, reading Makimuku as the seat of a confederated Wa kingship under Himiko.

items.title: Stone-lined coffin opened in the 'mysterious area' of Yoshinogari
items.note: A large, isolated late Yayoi cist with incised lid stones and red pigment revived Kyushu claims; reports indicated no grave goods were recovered.

items.title: Kōkogaku ga kaimei suru Yamataikoku no jidai (public symposium)
items.note: Symposium on mirrors, Lelang trade, Yayoi settlements and early mounded tombs, with Terasawa, Fukunaga, Okamura and others; published as a volume.

items.title: Ronsō Yamataikoku (The Yamatai debate)
items.note: Edited volume issued with the Japanese Archaeological Association that sets competing Kinai and Kyushu arguments alongside current evidence.

items.title: 3-seiki Harima no Wajin shokoku ni kansuru bunken shigaku・kōkogaku no tōgōteki kenkyū (Integrated textual and archaeological study of the third-century Wa states in Harima), KAKEN JP26K04293
items.note: JSPS grant (2026–2029, ¥1.56 million) testing the placement of Weizhi states between Tōma (Kibi) and Yamatai (Yamato) in Harima, with a re-edited Weizhi text.

items.title: Yamataikoku no kōkogaku: Gishi Tōiden ga kataru sekai
items.note: Archaeological study of the Yamatai period framed by the Wei zhi account of the eastern peoples and its wider East Asian setting.

items.title: Hashihaka kofun no myūon rajiogurafī ni yoru kenkyū (Muon radiography of the Hashihaka mound)
items.note: Reports non-invasive muon imaging of the Imperial Household Agency-controlled mound often proposed as Himiko's tomb, where excavation is not permitted.
